findings.summary: Both boxes in section 4 overflow: the client-side value is clipped by its box border and the server-side value is cut off at the right page edge.
findings.evidence: Client side box reads "credentials:'include" with the closing quote clipped at the box border; Server side box reads "'Allow-Credentials: tru" — the value "true" is truncated at the page edge (x ≈ 1080).
findings.fix: Let the code-styled values in the two comparison boxes wrap to a second line (or shrink their font size) so "credentials:'include'" and "Allow-Credentials: true" fit inside their box widths and inside the page margin.

findings.summary: The two long Vary header names in section 3 run past the left column and are clipped mid-token by the adjacent red callout box.
findings.evidence: "Vary: Access-Control-Request-Metho" — the trailing "d" of "Method" is cut where the "Cached Config Regression" box begins; the line above, "Vary: Access-Control-Request-Headers", also crosses the column boundary.
findings.fix: Allow the monospace header names in section 3 to wrap (e.g. break after "Vary:") or reduce their font size so both fit within the left column width.

findings.summary: The CORP values list in section 4 is cut off at the right page edge.
findings.evidence: "same-origin | same-site | cross-orig" — the final value "cross-origin" is truncated at the page boundary.
findings.fix: Wrap the CORP value list onto a second line or reduce its font size so "cross-origin" renders inside the right margin.

findings.summary: The Spring annotation in section 5 is cut off at the right page edge.
findings.evidence: "@CrossOrigin(origins="https://app.co" — the URL and closing parenthesis are truncated at the page boundary.
findings.fix: Wrap the annotation after "origins=" or place it in a code block that soft-wraps so the full "@CrossOrigin(origins=\"https://app.com\")" is visible.

findings.summary: The caption advertises a 10-part guide but only 9 titles exist.
findings.evidence: Caption: "This 10-part field guide walks the whole CORS handshake" — titles array contains 9 entries ("Same-Origin Policy: The Wall CORS Opens" … "Beyond Basic CORS: Redirects, Modes, and Neighbors").
findings.fix: Change "This 10-part field guide" to "This 9-part field guide", or add the missing tenth page so the count matches.

findings.summary: The Same-Origin Policy page ends with a preflight code example that uses "preflighted" and "OPTIONS" three pages before either term is defined.
findings.evidence: Page 1 final block: `// preflighted: JSON content-type` … `body:'{}'})  // OPTIONS fires first`. The two request flavors are first named on page 2 ("simple" / "preflighted" / "OPTIONS probe") and preflight is only defined on page 4 ("An automatic `OPTIONS` request the browser sends before the real one").
findings.fix: Delete this code block from page 1 (the page already closes cleanly on the "Mental Model" cloud callout) and move it to page 3 under "Two Concrete Calls", where the `application/json` preflight claim is actually taught.

findings.summary: The section 2 heading overlaps the "cross-origin fetch" box belonging to section 3.
findings.evidence: The heading "Access-Control-Allow-Origin" runs under the left border of the "cross-origin fetch" box, with "Origin" sitting behind the box outline.
findings.fix: Shorten or wrap the section 2 heading (e.g. break after "Access-Control-") or shift the section 3 flow box right/down so the two elements no longer occupy the same band.

findings.summary: The heading "Two Concrete Calls" is followed by only one call, leaving the page's central claim about JSON preflights with no example.
findings.evidence: Page 3: heading "Two Concrete Calls" is followed by a single code block — `// simple: no OPTIONS at all` / `fetch(u, {method:'POST', body: new URLSearchParams({a:1})})` — and then immediately by the heading "Why This Set Exists". The paired bullet "`application/json` is the #1 accidental preflight" is never demonstrated.
findings.fix: Add the preflighted counterpart under the same heading (the JSON-body `fetch` currently stranded on page 1), so the contrast the heading promises is actually shown.

findings.summary: The deck states the only limit on `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` is credentials mode, omitting that the wildcard never covers `Authorization` — which the bearer-token advice on page 6 then relies on.
findings.evidence: "`Allow-Headers: *` works only without credentials" and, on the credentials page, "It forces a preflight and needs `Allow-Headers`" … "So it dodges the wildcard trap entirely"
findings.fix: Add the exception: per the Fetch spec, `Authorization` is not covered by `*` in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` even on uncredentialed requests — it must always be listed by name (`Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization, content-type`). Amend the bearer-token Q&A accordingly.

findings.summary: The Express snippet uses `app.options('*', ...)`, which throws at boot on Express 5 (the current default major).
findings.evidence: "app.options('*', cors())  // if no auto OPTIONS"
findings.fix: Use an Express 5-valid wildcard: `app.options('/{*splat}', cors())` (or `/*splat` to exclude the root). In Express 5, path-to-regexp v8 rejects a bare `*` with `TypeError: Missing parameter name`.

findings.summary: The Private Network Access description is obsolete: Chrome replaced the server-header opt-in with the Local Network Access permission prompt (enforced in Chrome 142), so a local server can no longer opt in by responding to the preflight.
findings.evidence: "Adds `Access-Control-Request-Private-Network`" / "Local server must opt in explicitly"
findings.fix: Retitle to Local Network Access and say the *user* grants permission via a Chrome prompt to the calling site; note that the old PNA preflight header (`Access-Control-Request-Private-Network` / `Access-Control-Allow-Private-Network`) was abandoned as impractical because it required changes on every local device. Also note LNA covers loopback, RFC1918 ranges and `.local`.

findings.summary: The Private Network Access header name in section 1 runs into the Nginx code box in the right column.
findings.evidence: "Access-Control-Request-Private-Network" extends past the left column and the word "Network" is crossed by the dashed left border of the Nginx code block.
findings.fix: Wrap the header name onto its own line within the left column, or shrink its font size so it terminates before the right column begins.

findings.summary: The final callout names "the reflect-any-origin bug" as an already-known concept, but origin reflection is never defined or demonstrated anywhere in the part.
findings.evidence: Page 9 callout "Never In Production": "`CORS_ALLOW_ALL_ORIGINS = True` combined with credentials. It is the reflect-any-origin bug shipped as a config flag." No earlier page uses the word "reflect" or "reflection", or shows a server echoing an unvalidated `Origin` back with `Allow-Credentials: true`.
findings.fix: Gloss it inline in the callout — e.g. "it echoes any requesting origin back with credentials allowed, so any site can read authenticated responses" — or drop the label and state the effect directly.

findings.summary: The caption advertises a 10-part guide but the deck contains 9 slides.
findings.evidence: "This 10-part field guide walks the whole CORS handshake" — slides array has 9 entries (two of them `(cont.)` pages).
findings.fix: Change to "9-part" or add the missing part.

findings.summary: `document.domain` is called "removed, dead", but only Chromium disables it by default and even there it is restorable, while Firefox and Safari still support the setter.
findings.evidence: "`document.domain` relaxation: removed, dead"
findings.fix: Say "immutable by default in Chrome/Edge since 115 (re-enabled only with `Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?0`), deprecated everywhere else" instead of "removed, dead".

findings.summary: Claiming CORS only gates fetch/XHR reads is wrong: several subresource types require CORS by default, independently of COEP.
findings.evidence: "So CORS only gates `fetch`/XHR reads"
findings.fix: Qualify it: CORS also governs `@font-face` fetches, ES module scripts, `crossorigin` images used in canvas/WebGL, and cross-origin script error detail — legacy tag loads stayed permissive, but those newer surfaces are CORS-gated.

findings.summary: The abbreviation ACAO is used in the flow diagram before the header it stands for appears, and is never expanded anywhere.
findings.evidence: Page 2 diagram nodes: "JS `fetch`", "browser adds `Origin`", "server", "ACAO check", "JS reads or throws" — this precedes the heading "`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`". The string "ACAO" then carries pages 5, 6, 7 and 9 ("omit ACAO entirely", "A static `ACAO: *`") with no definition given.
findings.fix: Write the heading as "`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (ACAO)" and move it above the flow diagram, so the abbreviation is introduced before its first use.

findings.summary: The credentials table mixes an XHR API call into a column of fetch modes, so one row answers a different question than its column headers ask.
findings.evidence: Page 5 table headers `["Mode","Cookies sent?"]` with rows `["same-origin (default)","only same-origin"]`, `["include","yes, cross-origin"]`, `["omit","never"]`, and `["xhr.withCredentials = true","XHR equivalent"]` — the last row is not a mode and "XHR equivalent" is not an answer to "Cookies sent?".
findings.fix: Drop the fourth row from the table and state the XHR mapping in the bullets below it ("XHR equivalent of `include`: `xhr.withCredentials = true`").

findings.summary: The callout presents third-party cookie deprecation as an ongoing erosion of `SameSite=None; Secure`, but Google cancelled Chrome's deprecation (and the choice prompt) in April 2025.
findings.evidence: "Third-party cookie deprecation is eroding `None; Secure` too."
findings.fix: Rephrase to name the actual browsers: Safari (ITP) and Firefox (Total Cookie Protection) block third-party cookies by default, while Chrome kept them after abandoning deprecation in April 2025 — so `None; Secure` is unreliable rather than being phased out industry-wide.

findings.summary: The page opens with a bullet list whose referent — "Same ban" — is only stated in the closing callout of the previous page.
findings.evidence: Page 6 first block, with no heading above it: "Same ban hits `Allow-Headers: *` and `Allow-Methods: *`". The ban itself is page 5's last block: "With credentials, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is rejected outright."
findings.fix: Add a heading such as "The Ban Spreads" above the list and name the rule once ("the credentialed-mode wildcard ban also hits …") so the page stands on its own.

findings.summary: The page opens with a headless bullet list whose subject — the `Access-Control-Max-Age` header — lives on the previous page, so the first bullet has no actor.
findings.evidence: Page 7 first block, no heading: "Caches the preflight result, skipping the round trip" / "Cache key = (origin, URL, method, header set)". The heading "`Access-Control-Max-Age`" and its example response are the last two blocks of page 6.
findings.fix: Add a heading like "What `Max-Age` Caches" above this list, or restate the subject in the first bullet ("`Access-Control-Max-Age` caches the preflight result, skipping the round trip").

findings.summary: `http.cors()` is the no-arg form that Spring Security deprecated in 6.x and removed in 7.0.
findings.evidence: "Spring Security needs `http.cors()` or OPTIONS is rejected"
findings.fix: Write `http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())` (or `http.cors(cors -> cors.configurationSource(source))`) — the no-arg `cors()` no longer compiles on Spring Security 7.

findings.summary: The nginx preflight snippet uses the variable `$o`, which is never defined on the page and is not an nginx built-in.
findings.evidence: Page 9 nginx code: `add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin $o;` — no `map` block, `set` directive, or prose anywhere introduces `$o`.
findings.fix: Either use the built-in `$http_origin`, or show the allowlist `map $http_origin $o { default ""; "https://app.com" $http_origin; }` above the `if` block so the variable is defined before it is used.
